name: PT BISI International Tbk

frontmatter.title: BISI International — a hybrid-seed franchise the market prices as a run-off
frontmatter.summary: BISI's corn-seed margin halved and the shares trade at 0.4x book, below the net current assets in the business. The franchise, the net cash and the inventory are intact, and the mix path back toward the last actual margin is the most probable one: BUY with 66.5% total return on a Rp798 target. El Nino and the free-seed programme are the risks.
thesis: Revenue is growing again — nine-month sales rose to IDR1,267.7bn from IDR1,075.0bn — but the profit pool has moved: hybrid corn seed earned a gross profit of IDR92.5bn on IDR383.0bn of nine-month seed sales, against a segment margin of 40.8% for the whole of FY2025 and 69.6% in FY2024 [S2, S3].

The balance sheet, not the profit statement, is the story: net current assets and cash of IDR335.1bn are most of the IDR1,476.0bn market capitalisation, but the inventory is a seasonal seed pipeline — IDR872.7bn of corn seed was still in the field at the third quarter — not a hidden asset [S2, F15].

The recovery we model is a mix path, not a price bet: vegetable seed, IDR272.3bn of sales at a 58.6% gross margin, grows with the Chia Tai joint venture while corn seed normalises, and the blended margin recovers to 38.0% — still below the FY2025A actual [S3, F42].
On our numbers the shares are worth Rp798 against Rp492, 66.5% including the dividend, so the call is BUY; the DCF alone gives Rp935 and the asset backing sets the floor [S0].

The controlling Jiaravanon family holds just over half the shares with a free float of 12.4% — below the house minimum — and the stock trades IDR245.5m a day, so position size, not the theory, is the binding constraint [S0, S2].

catalysts.event: Close of the 2026/27 planting season and the government's free corn-seed distribution; the area actually planted sets the FY2027 seed order book
The statistical agency's January 2027 corn estimate and the FY2026 audited results; the fourth-quarter harvest is where the El Nino risk lands
Full-year 2026 accounts: the corn-seed segment gross margin and the inventory balance are the two lines that move our value
Annual general meeting and the FY2026 dividend declaration; the payout has been held near two fifths of profit through the downturn
First-half 2027 seed sales, the joint venture's first full vegetable-seed season, and the corn-seed margin against the 2026 trough

blocks.text: **BUY · target Rp798 · price Rp492 · total return 66.5%.** We initiate coverage of BISI at BUY. The company is the listed hybrid-seed and agri-input arm of the Jiaravanon family's Charoen Pokphand complex in Indonesia: it breeds and multiplies hybrid corn seed, vegetable and fruit seed and paddy seed through contract farmers, and distributes pesticides and fertilisers [S3]. The shares have fallen to a fraction of book — 0.4x — after the core corn-seed gross margin more than halved, from 69.6% in FY2024 to 40.8% in FY2025 and to a nine-month 2026 margin that the segment note puts at IDR92.5bn of gross profit on IDR383.0bn of seed sales [S2, S3].

Our variant view is that the market is treating a price-and-mix problem as a permanent one — wrongly. Volume is not collapsing: group sales rose to IDR1,267.7bn in the nine months to September 2026 from IDR1,075.0bn, and hybrid corn-seed sales rose faster still [S2]. What collapsed is the margin, because the seed crop was grown at 2024 input costs and sold into a market where the government is handing out free corn seed to livestock farmers on 300 thousand hectares [S7], and because the vegetable-seed line cut price -41.8% to grow volume 55.7% [S3]. Against that, the balance sheet is strong — no meaningful interest-bearing debt and cash of IDR335.1bn — and the board kept paying a dividend through two years of negative operating cash flow [S2, S3].

Three things move the value. First, the corn-seed gross margin: group revenue on our FY2026E numbers is IDR1,908.5bn, so every point of margin is real money, and we model a mix-led recovery to 38.0% rather than a return to the FY2024 peak. Second, working capital: inventory of IDR1,986.4bn is the single largest asset, and the path of that ratio is the difference between a value of about Rp935 and a value that clears the balance sheet. Third, the payout: at Rp22 of dividend on our FY2026E numbers the yield is 4.4%, and the board has paid every year of the downturn [S4].

We are buyers at Rp492 because the cash flows do get there, once the terminal value stops contradicting the cash flow it capitalises and the margin recovers to a level still below the last actual. Our DCF is worth Rp935 a share. The blended, liquidity-adjusted target is Rp798, which includes a 20.0% discount for a stock that trades IDR245.5m a day. The valuation section sets out why we have taken the P/B cross-check out of that blend, and what the target would be if we had not.

The seed business is a slow, technical franchise: a hybrid variety earns its keep for perhaps a decade, and the breeder who owns the germplasm collects a royalty-like margin in the years when the pipeline is fresh and the multiplication cost is under control. Distribution and farmer credit matter as much as genetics in a market where the buyer is a smallholder with limited cash.

BISI sells four things, and the mix explains the margin history. Hybrid corn seed was IDR499.3bn of FY2025 net sales, vegetable and fruit seed IDR272.3bn, pesticides and fertilisers IDR860.8bn, with a small paddy-seed line making up the rest [S3]. The agrochemical distribution business is therefore about half of revenue but a smaller share of gross profit: in the nine months to September 2026 the segment note shows the corn-seed line earning IDR92.5bn of gross profit while the agrochemical line earned more revenue on a thinner margin [S2]. This is not a pure seed company, and the valuation has to reflect that the largest revenue line is a distribution business with a working-capital appetite and a price-taking margin.

The corn-seed franchise is the reason to own the shares. FY2025 hybrid corn-seed volume grew 45.2% and the average selling price rose 7.5%, so the IDR499.3bn of seed revenue was earned on real volume, not on price alone [S3]. Seed is produced through contract farmers rather than on company-owned estates: BISI supplies the parent seed and the agronomy, the farmer grows the crop, and the company conditions, treats and bags it. The annual report describes the shift toward contract farmers and toward higher-margin products as the core of the FY2025 operating model, supported by large-scale demonstration plots managed by internal agronomists to pull demand through the channel [S3]. In the agrochemical line, volume grew 37.4% while the average selling price fell -10.7% — the signature of a distribution business passing through a falling input price [S3].

The mix is a price story in two of the three lines, and that is the part earlier drafts left out. In vegetable and fruit seed — IDR272.3bn of FY2025 sales at a 58.6% gross margin, the highest in the group — the average selling price fell -41.8% while volume rose 55.7% [S3]. In agrochemicals, volume grew 37.4% while the average selling price fell -10.7% [S3]. Two of the three segments are buying volume with price, which makes the margin collapse structural rather than a one-year corn-seed cost problem, and it is why the base case recovers the blended margin to 38.0% rather than to the FY2025A level.

Research is the moat and it is expensed, not capitalised. R&D expense was IDR102.7bn in FY2025, a little over six per cent of sales, spent on the breeding pipeline that produces the varieties the contract farmers multiply [S3]. The company also runs the relationship with Chia Tai Seeds of Thailand, an entity under common control: they signed a breeding research agreement in 2023, and on 7 January 2026 the two established PT Dwidaya Tani Mandiri, a horticultural-seed joint venture in which BISI holds the majority and Chia Tai the balance, with paid-up capital of ten billion rupiah, to produce and distribute vegetable and fruit seed in Indonesia [S3]. That is small money, but it is the direction of travel: horticulture is where the higher-margin genetics sit.

The group is controlled by the Jiaravanon family, which the quarterly filing names as the controlling shareholder [S2]. PT Agrindo Pratama holds 31.0% of the shares and three Singapore investment vehicles — Field, Valley and Vista Investment Holdings — hold a further tranche each, taking the family block to just over half the company [S2]. The free float is 12.4% and institutions hold 10.9% [S0]. The company employs 1,247.0 people [S0]. BISI is the listed seed and agri-input vehicle of that group; the related-party note shows seed, side-product and pesticide sales into the group's feed and farming operations [S3].

BISI is an established breeder, not the new entrant, in hybrid corn seed, with its own germplasm and a national dealer network; the competitive set includes the Indonesian subsidiaries of global seed houses and a long tail of local multipliers. We cannot source a market-share number, and we do not use one: the report treats BISI as a scaled challenger with a technical edge in corn and a distribution business attached, rather than as the price-setter in either line [S3].

The demand driver is planted area and hybrid adoption, and both are moving slowly in the company's favour. Indonesia's corn output reached 13.16m tonnes in the first nine months of 2026, up on the same period a year earlier, but September output fell and the statistical agency expects the fourth-quarter harvest to be weaker on an El Nino that it describes as stronger than the 2023 episode [S6]. That matters twice over: less domestic corn means less seed sold into the next planting, while a higher corn price is good for the farmer's willingness to pay for a hybrid. The national corn price at farmer level was at the bottom of a range that sits above the government's reference price at the end of 2025, so farmer economics still support buying seed rather than saving grain [S3].

Policy is the swing factor and it cuts against the commercial seed trade at the low end. The agriculture ministry has budgeted IDR600.0bn for free corn seed to livestock farmers across 300 thousand hectares, half of it in 2026 and half in 2027, with an output target the ministry puts above the feed sector's annual requirement [S7]. Separately, the ministry has bought hybrid seed outright for distribution to farmers at no charge [S5]. Free seed does not eliminate the commercial market — the quality and yield of the subsidised material are a different proposition from a bought hybrid, and the demonstration-plot model exists precisely to prove that — but it caps what BISI can charge at the entry end, which is why we hold the long-run corn-seed margin well below its FY2024 level [S7, S3].

The revenue history shows how much of this business is a price cycle wearing a volume disguise. Group net sales were IDR2,415.6bn in FY2022A and IDR2,298.1bn in FY2023A, then IDR1,367.9bn in FY2024A, a change of -40.5%, and IDR1,696.4bn in FY2025A [S0]. A seed business does not lose two fifths of its revenue in a year because farmers stopped planting; the agrochemical distribution line, half of the group, marked down with the global fertiliser and crop-protection price after the 2022-23 spike, and the segment review describes exactly that pass-through, with selective price adjustments to hold share [S3]. Our read, and the reason we model a normalised rather than a peak margin, is that the FY2023A gross margin of 50.6% was a restocking windfall, not an earning power.

The structural picture is a market that grows with area and yield, in the low single digits by volume, with value growth from mix and from the farmer's willingness to pay for genetics. Four forces set the margin. Buyers are fragmented smallholders, so there is no customer concentration, but the channel is expensive and credit-heavy. Suppliers of parent seed and agrochemical active ingredients are concentrated and mostly foreign, so input costs move with the rupiah — the macro deck carries the dollar at 18,350 for FY2027E, and every rupiah of depreciation raises the cost of imported intermediates [S3]. New entrants face a breeding cycle measured in years, a real barrier, but the incumbent global seed houses have deeper pipelines. Substitutes are saved seed and free government seed, and both are live threats at the low end [S7].

The moat is therefore narrower than the R&D spend implies: a germplasm library, a contract-farming base and a dealer network, none of which is a licence, a resource or a switching cost for the farmer. That justifies a valuation on cash flow and asset value rather than on any franchise multiple, and it is why we do not carry a commodity NAV for this name — there is no commodity output and no benchmark price, so the plantation method does not apply [S3]. The agri deck in our library prices crude palm oil, corn, soybean meal and wheat, and nothing in it prices a bag of hybrid corn seed; the closest series is corn itself, at 215 for FY2027E against a spot of 176, and it is the crop that sets both seed demand and the seed-corn input cost. It does not reach this model, and we will not pretend otherwise: the corporate template builds revenue from growth and a gross margin and has no commodity-price linkage, so the model's drivers are entirely company-specific and the deck reads nothing on this name. We use the deck as context — the rupiah at 18,350 and the corn price path are the two external variables that would move the inputs — not as model inputs, and the risks they carry are set out in the risk section not carried in a formula [S3].

The five-year record is a margin cycle with a working-capital problem attached. Revenue went IDR2,415.6bn, IDR2,298.1bn, IDR1,367.9bn, IDR1,696.4bn, and we forecast IDR1,908.5bn for FY2026E [S0]. Gross margin went 42.2%, 50.6%, 47.3%, 40.1% and 33.5% on our numbers, and the EBITDA margin went from 30.8% at the cycle peak to 16.7% in FY2025A and 13.5% in FY2026E [S0, S3].

Two restatements matter before any of those numbers can be used. The data pack's depreciation line is a fraction of the real charge; the notes to the FY2025 accounts show total depreciation charged of IDR55.7bn, split across cost of goods sold, selling, general and administrative and research expense, against IDR52.9bn in FY2024 [S3]. The pack's operating profit is also wrong because it does not carry the other-operating lines inside EBIT: the audited operating profit is IDR226.9bn in FY2025 and IDR206.3bn in FY2024 [S3, F48/F49], so we restate it from the income statement. We take the note figure as the model's D&A and the audited figure as EBIT: EBITDA is IDR282.7bn on IDR1,696.4bn of sales, 16.7%, and IDR257.6bn in FY2026E. Everything in the valuation depends on those corrections; on the pack's figures the company would look both less cash-generative and more profitable at the operating line than it is [S3, F2, F3].

The forecast is a recovery in margin, a slowdown in growth and a release of working capital, in that order. Revenue grows 12.5% in FY2026E to IDR1,908.5bn, then 4.0% — held below national output growth because the 2026/27 season is the one El Nino shortens, and the statistical agency already guides the fourth-quarter harvest lower [S6, F34]. Growth then runs 6.0% to 5.0% on hybrid adoption and the vegetable-seed line, and tapers to the terminal rate through FY2035E rather than entering the perpetuity at a higher trajectory [S3]. Gross margin recovers from 33.5% to 35.0% in FY2027E and 38.0% by FY2030E — and this is the change in this revision, so we set out the mechanism rather than asserting it. The recovery is a mix path, not a price bet, and it lands 38.0% against the FY2025A actual of 40.1% — below the last actual, but by a distance the agrochemical weight explains, not by an unexplained haircut [S0]. The vegetable and fruit seed line, IDR272.3bn of FY2025 sales, earned a 58.6% gross margin while corn seed earned 40.8% [S3]; the Chia Tai horticultural joint venture established on 7 January 2026 exists to grow exactly that line, so its weight in the blend rises while the corn-seed margin normalises from a nine-month IDR92.5bn of gross profit on IDR383.0bn of sales toward the 40.8% it earned in FY2025 [S3, S2]. Clearing the high-cost crop does not by itself lift a margin — we sold that argument in the first draft and it was wrong — the lift comes from the mix and from the seed crop grown for the 2027 season costing less than the 2026 one, which the FY2025 annual report's own input-cost commentary supports but does not quantify [S3]. Operating expense falls from 23.3% of sales to 21.5% on fixed-cost leverage alone, with R&D held in real terms rather than cut [S3]. The FY2026E level is built from the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the prior-year quarter's absolute cost, not by applying the nine-month ratio to full-year revenue: the fourth quarter carries about a third of sales against a quarter of the year's expense, and the nine-month absolute cost fell while sales rose [S2, F18/F45, S3]. At a similar sales level in FY2023 the company ran a lower ratio still, so the path assumes no cost-cutting, only that the cost base does not grow with revenue it does not need [S0]. Net profit is IDR153.8bn in FY2026E, IDR189.1bn in FY2027E and IDR310.0bn by FY2030E, with earnings per share of Rp51 rising to Rp103.

The cash flow is where the last three years went wrong, and where the next three years are decided. Operating cash flow was negative in FY2025, IDR-263.2bn, after IDR-146.3bn the year before, and the annual report attributes it to the inventory build: inventories rose IDR512.6bn, or about a third, in a single year [S3]. Free cash flow to the firm was negative in FY2023A, FY2024A and FY2025A — IDR-333.4bn in the last of them — because the change in working capital absorbed IDR493.0bn [S0]. Our forecast has working capital falling from the FY2025A level to IDR2,232.9bn in FY2026E, a ratio of 117.0% of revenue, against IDR2,306.0bn on IDR1,696.4bn of sales in FY2025A. That easing is already visible: inventory stayed flat at IDR1,969.4bn while nine-month revenue rose to IDR1,267.7bn [S2]. The ratio then slides to 103.0% by FY2030E, and that release is a large part of the FY2026E free cash flow of IDR200.1bn.

Capex is maintenance. Fixed-asset additions were IDR80.1bn in FY2025 and we carry 4.6% of revenue, enough for seed-conditioning and processing capacity without an expansion project [S3, F37]. The balance sheet is the strongest part of the case: no meaningful borrowings at the third quarter, cash of IDR335.1bn, and equity of IDR3,482.2bn, with the seasonal seed crop funded from the company's own resources [S2]. Net debt at FY2025A was a surplus of IDR-149.9bn and on our numbers the surplus widens to IDR-648.1bn by FY2030E. There is no refinancing risk, no covenant and no minority of any size [S2].

Capital allocation is a dividend and retained cash. The board declared Rp26 a share for FY2025, 41.0% of profit attributable to the parent, having paid a higher dividend in FY2024A, and has paid every year of the cycle [S4, S0]. We model a 42.0% payout throughout, which gives Rp22 in FY2026E and Rp26 in FY2027E, and leaves the net cash position to build rather than to be deployed. No rights issue, no buyback and no change in the share count are assumed [S2].

Earnings quality. The first flag is cash conversion, and it is the serious one. Net profit has outrun operating cash flow in each of the last two years — IDR190.3bn of profit against IDR-263.2bn of operating cash flow, after the prior year's IDR-146.3bn — which on the group's balance sheet is an accruals-to-average-total-assets ratio above the house's ten per cent warning line in FY2025 and close to it in FY2024 — the trend matters more than the level, and it has stopped worsening. We classify it as optics-class, not manipulation-class: the accrual is an inventory build of IDR512.6bn disclosed by category and explained in the annual report's own cash-flow commentary [S3], the receivables balance is falling rather than growing, and the build reverses in the forecast because inventory was flat year-to-date while nine-month sales rose to IDR1,267.7bn from IDR1,075.0bn [S2, F14/F16]. The second flag is inventory: IDR1,986.4bn of stock at the end of FY2025 is more than half of total assets, and the note shows IDR872.7bn of corn seed still in the field at the third quarter of 2026 [S2]. We treat that as a seasonal pipeline rather than a markdown candidate, because it is work-in-process in the ground, but a failed harvest or a collapse in seed demand would turn it into a write-down, and the bear case carries it.

The related-party test is small enough to be an optics flag. Sales to related parties were IDR5.0bn in FY2025 — 0.3% of net sales — and the receivable that sits behind them is smaller again; both are disclosed by counterparty in the related-party note with a fairness opinion on the affiliated transactions [S3]. We use the flow rather than the receivable because the receivable tells you about the balance outstanding, not about how much of the business moves inside the group.

Against those, the working-capital trend is improving: receivables turnover rose to 3.6x in FY2025 from a much longer collection period the year before, and the third-quarter cash balance recovered to IDR335.1bn from IDR166.7bn at the prior year-end [S3, S2]. There is no special-monitoring-board status or notation letter in the filings we hold, no change of auditor and no restatement [S2, S3, S4].

We value BISI on a ten-year FCFF DCF as the primary method, with an EV/EBITDA cross-check and no P/B leg. The DCF leads because the business is a going concern with a normalisable margin, one currency, no material debt and no commodity output: there is no reserve, no benchmark price and no NAV to discount, so the plantation method in our industry config does not fit, and a corporate FCFF model with a working-capital line is the honest way to capture both the margin recovery and the cash release [S3]. The terminal value is 51.8% of the DCF value, high but within the range a ten-year franchise model produces. Terminal growth is 3.0%, and the explicit years taper into it: revenue growth tapers in equal steps over FY2031E-FY2035E from the last explicit rate to the 3.0% perpetuity, so the FY2035E free cash flow that the Gordon formula capitalises embeds the same growth rate the formula applies to it — including its working-capital build, which is IDR82.6bn — the 100.0% working-capital ratio applied to a revenue increment growing at the terminal rate rather than at the faster explicit rate it would otherwise carry [S0]. An earlier draft applied the terminal rate to a faster-growing cash flow; that understated the DCF by the working-capital difference alone and it is corrected here, not carried.

The cost of capital is built from the house macro inputs rather than from a measured beta. The ten-year rupiah risk-free rate is 7.4%, the country default spread 1.6%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2% and the country risk premium 2.5%, with an unlevered beta of 0.80 — the plantation default, stated explicitly because no measured beta exists for this industry in our library [S0]. With no net debt the levered beta is the same, the cost of equity is 11.2% and the WACC is 11.2%. A higher beta or a bigger country premium would on its own take the DCF below the current price; we do not think the evidence supports either, because the revenue is domestic and the balance sheet is in rupiah.

The DCF gives Rp935 a share. The two assumptions we are least sure of are the long-run gross margin and the working-capital ratio, and they pull in the same direction: a one-point change in the long-run gross margin moves the value by about seven per cent, and a ten-point change in the working-capital ratio by about five. The FY2026E free cash flow of IDR200.1bn is flattered by the working-capital release and should not be annualised; the model's steady-state free cash flow is closer to the FY2030E figure of IDR222.5bn. We do not publish a sensitivity grid: the engine builds its tariff from the industry config, whose axes are a palm-oil benchmark, a volume driver and a strip ratio, none of which this model carries, so every cell of that exhibit prints the undiscounted base target and tells a reader the value is insensitive to everything. Rather than print a flat table, we say what the engine will not: the grid does not exist for a corporate-template name, and the margin and working-capital sensitivities above are the ones to weigh.

The EV/EBITDA cross-check gives Rp793, -15.2% above the DCF, at an exit multiple of 7.3x on FY2025A EBITDA of IDR282.7bn — the audited year to December 2025 on the restated operating profit and the note D&A, which is the engine's metric, not LTM. The label matters and an earlier draft got it wrong. On the other two plausible bases the leg is lower: LTM operating profit on the same restated basis is FY2025A IDR226.9bn less the nine months of 2025 (IDR99.6bn) plus the nine months of 2026 (IDR79.2bn), and with the restated D&A run-rate it gives an LTM EBITDA below the FY2025A figure, and FY2026E EBITDA is IDR257.6bn, the trough. At the same multiple the FY2026E basis would put the leg materially below the DCF, not above it, and the blend at a quarter weight would fall by roughly the difference; the target would still clear the price by more than the house ADD threshold, so the rating does not rest on the stale metric. We keep the leg at a quarter weight because a multiple is how a small-capitalisation agri-input company is actually traded, but we do not believe the level: the multiple is the average of a peer set that is mostly crude-palm planters and of BISI's own history, and both were earned when the company was producing a return on equity in the high teens. Applying it to today's trough EBITDA double-counts the recovery. The market is paying 4.7x EV/EBITDA for FY2026E and 7.8x FY2027E earnings, the right order of magnitude for a business earning single-digit returns [S0].

We have therefore dropped the P/B leg, the only departure from the industry config. At the third-quarter equity attributable to the owners of the parent of IDR3,482.2bn, or Rp1,161 a share, return on equity is 4.4% on our FY2026E numbers and 7.5% by FY2030E, against a cost of equity of 11.2%. A justified P/B on that return and a three per cent growth rate is a small fraction of book, roughly a quarter of it, and the market itself pays 0.4x. Capitalising BISI at a planter's multiple of book would add about a fifth to our target, and would be the single largest error in this report if we kept it: it would capitalise a return level the company does not earn from a multiple earned in a different industry.

What the balance sheet is worth, stated plainly, is a floor rather than a target. Net current assets at 30 September 2026 are current assets less current liabilities, and with cash of IDR335.1bn inside them and no meaningful debt they exceed the market capitalisation: the shares trade below the working capital in the business, not merely below book, at 0.4x of Rp1,190 of book [S2, F32]. We do not run that as a valuation case, for one reason we can source: IDR1,986.4bn of the inventory is at cost, and IDR872.7bn of it is corn seed still in the field at the third quarter [S2, F15]. Seed work-in-process has no second-use value if the variety fails or the season is lost — it is not a commodity stock that can be sold at a discount — so the realisable value in a forced case is the saleable seed, not the book number. Our bull case is therefore where the asset backing does its work: a normal season and a working joint venture are what convert the working capital into cash, and the bull value of Rp1,160 is the case in which the inventory turns rather than marks down.

The blended value before the liquidity adjustment is Rp900, the twelve-month target before the discount is Rp979, and after subtracting the dividend we assume is paid over the year and applying a 20.0% discount for a stock whose three-month average daily traded value is IDR245.5m — below the threshold at which the house stops discounting — the published target is Rp798. That is 62.1% of price appreciation plus Rp22 of dividend, 66.5% in total. The discount is not a view on the business: it is the cost of building and exiting a position in a name with a 12.4% free float.

What the price implies. At Rp492 the market is paying 9.6x our FY2026E earnings, 0.4x book and 4.7x EV/EBITDA, and getting a 4.4% yield. That is well below the DCF value of Rp935 and below the multiple cross-check: at this price the market is capitalising the trough year indefinitely, not a mid-cycle seed franchise. The engine's reverse DCF cannot price this name — it searches on the palm-oil benchmark, which this model does not use — so we solved the implied drivers by hand on the engine's own sensitivities. Holding the long-run margin at our 38.0%, the Rp492 price implies a working-capital ratio near twice revenue rather than the 100.0% we model; holding our working capital, it implies a long-run gross margin below even the 33.5% FY2026E trough — the market is disputing the recovery, not merely its pace. The gap therefore sits in the margin path and the cash release, not in the growth rate: the market is pricing the trough margin, or a permanent working-capital sink, as the long run. We think the most probable path is the recovery we model, which is why this initiation carries a BUY call — a change from the HOLD of the first draft of this report, after the model was rebuilt on a fixed-cost operating base rather than a nine-month ratio carried into a fourth quarter that carries a third of the year's sales; the recovery is still below the FY2025A margin even at its end point, so it is not a bull case smuggled into the base.

A seed company at a low-teens return on equity should trade below book unless the market expects the return to rise. The reverse is what makes agri-input names look optically cheap at the bottom of a margin cycle, and it is the trap in this sector.

**Regulatory and policy (likelihood high, impact high).** Free government corn seed across 300 thousand hectares, with half the budget still to be spent in 2027, is a direct substitute at the entry end of the market, and the ministry's output target implies a substantial area coming out of the commercial seed channel [S7]. A cheaper, more aggressive subsidy is the single most credible way our margin recovery fails. A reference-price intervention on corn would work the other way, by supporting the farmer's ability to pay [S3].

**Weather and volume (likelihood medium, impact high).** The statistical agency already reports a weaker September harvest and expects the fourth quarter to be worse on an El Nino stronger than the 2023 episode [S6]. A delayed or shortened 2026/27 planting season cuts seed volume twice: once in the seed order book and once in the farmer's cash. That is why FY2027E growth in the base case is 4.0%, below the national output trend, and why the bear case takes a further three points off growth rather than only the margin [S6].

**Input cost and currency (likelihood medium, impact medium).** Parent seed, agrochemical active ingredients and packaging are imported or import-priced. The macro deck carries the rupiah at 18,350 for FY2027E, and a sustained depreciation raises cost of goods sold with a lag while the subsidised competitor caps the pass-through [S3]. This is the channel through which a macro shock reaches a domestic revenue line.

**Inventory and earnings quality (likelihood medium, impact medium).** IDR1,986.4bn of inventory, IDR872.7bn of it corn seed in the field at the third quarter, against equity of IDR3,482.2bn [S2]. A markdown of even a tenth of the seed work-in-process would take a visible bite out of a year in which we forecast IDR153.8bn of net profit, which is why the bear case's margin shock is sized to carry it rather than left as a sentence.

**Governance, free float and related parties (likelihood low, impact medium).** The family holds just over half the shares and the free float is 12.4% [S2, S0, F33]. That number fails the exchange's minimum: IDX Rule I-A, in force 31 March 2026, raised the public-float floor from seven and a half per cent to fifteen per cent, and gives issuers with a market capitalisation below five trillion rupiah until 31 March 2029 to comply [S8]. BISI, at a market capitalisation of IDR1,476.0bn, is inside that final tier and short of the floor today. The remediation route is a controlling-shareholder sell-down or a placement of existing shares, and it cuts both ways: it fixes the liquidity discount we apply but adds supply, and a placement at a discount to market is the usual form. Sales into the group's feed and farming businesses are disclosed by counterparty and are genuinely small — 0.3% of net sales — and the affiliated transactions carry a fairness opinion [S3]. The risk is not today's flows but the absence of a minority veto over future ones, plus the supply overhang a remediation would create; that is a valuation discount rather than a forecast.

**Liquidity (likelihood certain, impact medium).** IDR245.5m of daily traded value [S0]. A position of any size takes weeks to build and longer to exit, which is why the target carries a 20.0% discount and why the house flags the name as not investable at full size.

Our three cases are mirrored on the same three drivers — gross margin, revenue growth and the working-capital ratio — in equal and opposite amounts, because those are the lines the evidence actually moves. The bear case, at a quarter probability, holds revenue growth three points below plan on the shortened 2026/27 season, takes three points off gross margin, and adds to the assumed working-capital intensity to reflect a seed crop that does not clear; the margin shock carries the markdown of the corn seed in the field, because a one-off write-down has no line in a driver model and folding it into the persistent margin is the conservative way to carry it — it is worth IDR872.7bn of work-in-process marked down by a tenth, against FY2025A net profit of IDR190.3bn. That case is worth Rp872. The base case, at one half, recovers the mix and releases cash, and is worth Rp979. The bull case, at a quarter, gets a normal monsoon, three points of extra volume, a margin back toward the FY2025A level with inventory normalising faster, and the working-capital intensity falling by the same eight points the bear adds; it is worth Rp1,160. The probabilities are judgement, not measurement. The bear is not a crop failure and the bull is not a return to the FY2024 seed margin: both are the same three drivers moved the same distance either way.

What would change our view, in either direction. On the downside: a second consecutive year of corn-seed gross margin near the 2026 level, a fourth-quarter harvest materially below the statistical agency's current expectation, an inventory provision, or a cut in the dividend. On the upside: evidence that the free-seed programme is confined to the livestock-feed corridor rather than the commercial market, a corn-seed margin back above the FY2025 level in the second half of 2027, or a working-capital ratio that falls toward our FY2028E assumption a year early. Any of those would move the DCF by more than the multiple cross-check, which is why we watch the segment note every quarter.

Control sits with the Jiaravanon family, which the quarterly filing names as the controlling shareholder, through PT Agrindo Pratama at 31.0% and three Singapore investment vehicles holding a further tranche each, for a block of just over half the company [S2]. The free float is 12.4% and the reported insider holding is 62.7% [S0]. No share pledge is disclosed in the share register of the third-quarter filing [S2]. There is no holding structure outside the operating group, no dual-class stock and no shareholder agreement disclosed in the filings we hold; the company has never done a rights issue and the share count has not changed [S2, S3].

Related-party dealings are the item to watch, and the disclosure is better than the index norm. The annual report lists sales of seed, side products, pesticides and rentals to the group's feed and farming companies by counterparty: IDR5.0bn in FY2025, 0.3% of net sales, with the resulting receivable disclosed in the same note, and it carries a fairness opinion on the affiliated transactions [S3]. Related-party sales as a share of revenue are the quantitative test, and 0.3% keeps this an optics flag rather than a manipulation flag — the flow is real, disclosed, priced at arm's length by opinion, and too small to move a year's profit. The Chia Tai joint venture is itself a related-party transaction — Chia Tai Seeds is an entity under common control — priced at a few billion rupiah for a majority stake in a ten-billion-rupiah vehicle, which is immaterial but shows the mechanism by which value could move inside the group [S3].

Free float is a governance constraint as much as a liquidity one. IDX Rule I-A requires a fifteen per cent public float and BISI is at 12.4%, below the minimum, with its market capitalisation inside the sub-five-trillion-rupiah tier whose compliance deadline is 31 March 2029 [S8]. The likely remediation is a sale of existing shares by the family block or a placement, which would add supply to a stock that already trades IDR245.5m a day; a placement would also be the point at which the family's control falls below half, so the incentive is to keep it small and orderly. We have not seen a filing that announces one, and we do not forecast one [S2].

Audit and reporting. The FY2025 accounts were audited by KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, and the same firm was reappointed for FY2026 at the annual general meeting [S4]. We found no auditor change, no restatement, no qualification and no late filing in the archive [S3, S4]. The third-quarter accounts are unaudited, as the regulation allows, and the fourth quarter is where the true-ups land — a point that matters for a company whose annual margin swing was as large as this one's [S2].

Dividends and capital returns. The board declared Rp26 for FY2025, 41.0% of attributable profit, having paid a higher dividend in FY2024A and through the negative-cash-flow years before that [S4, S0]. The policy is a stable cash payout rather than a fixed ratio, and the net cash position means it is at risk from a decision to retain cash for the seed crop rather than from refinancing [S2]. There is no buyback and no treasury stock.

ESG. The environmental exposure is agricultural rather than industrial: seed multiplication is done by contract farmers, so the direct footprint is processing and conditioning plants, and the annual report frames sustainability around farmer productivity, demonstration plots and agronomist advisory programmes [S3]. The social dimension is the material one — smallholder incomes, farmer credit and the adoption of hybrids that raise yield per hectare — and it is also the commercial model. The governance dimension is the concentrated family control described above, mitigated by a small related-party flow and an independent-commissioner structure we have not tested in detail. Climate risk is direct and rising: an El Nino stronger than 2023 is already in the statistical agency's fourth-quarter guidance, and it hits both the seed crop and the farmer's ability to buy [S6]. We do not apply a separate ESG discount; the weather risk is inside the bear case.

The dated catalysts are the planting season, the statistics and the dividend. The 2026/27 season closes at the end of December 2026, and the area planted under the free-seed programme is the first hard evidence on whether the subsidy displaces commercial seed [S7]. The statistical agency's January 2027 corn estimate and the FY2026 audited accounts carry the fourth-quarter harvest and the year's true-up [S6]. The annual general meeting and the FY2026 dividend declaration follow in the second quarter of 2027. The Chia Tai horticultural joint venture contributes inside FY2026, not 1H2027: it was established by deed on 7 January 2026 and its subscription is already in the 30 September 2026 balance sheet, so the seed sales of the 2027 season — booked in the first half — are its second contribution, not its first [S3].

Between updates we monitor five lines: the hybrid corn-seed gross margin in the quarterly segment note, the single number that moves our value; the split of corn-seed revenue between volume and price, because volume growth with a falling price is a different business from price growth; the inventory and work-in-process balance, with IDR872.7bn of corn seed in the field at the last reading; the free-seed programme's area and budget execution against the IDR600.0bn allocated; and the payout, as the signal that the family is content to distribute the group's cash [S2, S3, S7]. The stock's own liquidity is the sixth: at IDR245.5m a day, an exit is a project, not a trade [S0].

valuation.basis: average of peer median and own five-year average

bear.narrative: El Nino shortens the 2026/27 planting season and free government seed takes share at the low end: seed volume falls 3pp below plan, the corn-seed crop in the field is marked down (the Rp87bn one-tenth of the corn work-in-process, folded into the -3pp margin shock because the engine has no one-off line), and the margin never recovers past the 2026 trough while working capital keeps absorbing cash.

bull.narrative: A normal 2027 monsoon, the food-self-sufficiency drive and the new BISI 234/235/236 varieties lift hybrid corn seed volumes 3pp above plan; the horticultural joint venture grows the 58.6%-margin vegetable-seed line faster than the agrochemical distribution, gross margin returns to the FY2025 40% level, and inventory normalises faster. Net current assets of roughly Rp2.5trn against the market capitalisation are the floor in this case, not the target.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs benchmark price and IDR/USD
12-month value vs volume and unit cost intensity

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +12.5%: 9M-2026 net sales were IDR 1,267.7bn vs IDR 1,075.0bn (+17.9%) [F16/F17], but the third quarter alone was flat-to-down and BPS reports September corn output -6.46% with a weaker Q4 harvest on a stronger El Nino [F34], so Q4-2026 is held to +3% on Q4-2025 revenue, giving about IDR 1,908bn for the year. FY2027E +4.0%: the 2026/27 season is the one El Nino shortens — BPS guides the fourth-quarter harvest lower and the planted area for the seed order book follows it down [S6] — so growth is held below national output growth of 2.73% plus price only because the vegetable-seed line grows with the Chia Tai joint venture [S3]. FY2028E-FY2030E +6.0/5.5/5.0%: national corn output grew 2.73% in the first nine months of 2026 [F34], hybrid adoption and agrochemical price inflation add the rest, and the government is distributing free corn seed on 300,000 ha, which caps the volume upside at the low end of the market [F35]. FY2031E-FY2035E taper 5.0/4.5/4.0/3.5/3.0% into the terminal rate: a mature franchise must not enter a 3.0% perpetuity from a 5.0% revenue trajectory, because the terminal FCFF would then be a different cash flow from the one the Gordon formula capitalises. Long-run 3.0% = 2.5% IDR inflation (macro deck) plus 0.5% real, equal to terminal growth.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 33.5%: 9M-2026 gross profit was IDR 398.3bn on IDR 1,267.7bn = 31.4% vs 41.4% a year earlier [F18/F19], with hybrid corn seed down to 24.1% from 49.2% [F23/F24] and the agrochemical mix (50.7% of FY2025 revenue at a 38% margin) now larger [F10]. Q4 is seasonally the strongest gross-margin quarter, so the full year is held slightly above the nine-month print. FY2027E 35.0%, FY2028E 36.5%, FY2029E 37.5%, FY2030E 38.0%: the recovery is a mix path, not a price bet. The vegetable and fruit seed line earned a 58.64% gross margin in FY2025 and its volume grew 55.66% [F7/F40/F41]; the Chia Tai horticultural joint venture established on 7 Jan 2026 exists to grow exactly that line [S3], so its weight in the blend rises while corn seed normalises from a 24.1% nine-month trough toward the 40.8% it earned in FY2025 [F7/F23]. The FY2025A blended margin of 40.1% is the ceiling we approach from below, not a level we haircut: 38.0% is the blend of a corn-seed line still below its FY2025 margin at a 29% weight, vegetable seed at its FY2025 margin at a rising weight, and agrochemicals at their FY2025 gross margin of 37.8% (325.760 of gross profit on 860.774 of external sales, S3 p.165) at roughly half of revenue. 36% would have been 4.1pp below the last actual with no mix path to justify it; 38.0% is 2.1pp below, which the agrochemical weight explains.

assumptions.label: SG&A and other opex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 23.3%: built from a fixed-cost base, not the nine-month ratio. 9M-2026 SG&A was IDR 326.702bn (selling 180.819 + G&A 79.748 + R&D 66.135); the fourth quarter is held at Q4-2025 SG&A of IDR 117.8bn (FY2025 SG&A 433.345 less 9M-2025 315.545) with no net other-operating item in Q4 — 9M-2026 ran +7.5bn of net other income and Q4-2025 +9.8bn, so this does not flatter — giving IDR 444.5bn, 23.3% of FY2026E sales [S2, F18/F45; S3 p.88]. The nine-month absolute expense fell 7.7% year on year while revenue rose 17.9%, and Q4 carries 34% of revenue against a quarter of the year's opex, so applying the nine-month ratio to the full year manufactures a Q4 step-up no source shows. The absolute cost is then held in real terms (+3%/yr, the macro deck's CPI), which is why the ratio falls as revenue rebuilds: FY2023, at a similar sales level, ran 468.0bn of opex on 2,298.1bn of revenue, 20.4%, so the path sits inside the company's own history and assumes no cost-cutting. The net other-operating charge stays inside the base, including inventory impairment of IDR 26.894bn in FY2025 and 29.455bn in FY2024 [S3 p.158, note 29]. Long-run 20.5%, the FY2035E ratio implied by the same 3% real growth.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at 3.3% of revenue, the FY2025 actual: depreciation charged was IDR 55.7bn on IDR 1,696.4bn of sales [F2/F1]. This is the restated figure from the LK notes (COGS + selling + G&A + R&D), not the IDR 16.3bn selling-expense slice the data pack carries.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: 4.6% of revenue: FY2025 cash capex was IDR 73.1bn (4.3% of sales) and fixed-asset additions IDR 80.1bn (4.7%) [F37]; 9M-2026 capex was IDR 90.8bn, about 4.8% annualised. Seed processing and conditioning plants need steady maintenance capex; no expansion project is assumed beyond that.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 117%: at 30 Sep 2026 operating working capital ex-cash was IDR 2,213.9bn — current assets 2,769.856 less cash 335.086 less current liabilities 220.889, where current liabilities are total liabilities 278.832 less non-current 57.943, and debt is nil at the date because the 16.806bn bank loan shown in note 13 was repaid in January 2026 — against LTM revenue of IDR 1,889.1bn = 1.17x, the data pack's own latest_bs.nwc line [S2, F31]. That is down from 1.36x at FY2025A on the same definition [S3]. The intensity is structural: IDR 1,149.8bn of the IDR 1,989.1bn gross inventory is work-in-process, including IDR 872.7bn of corn seed still in the field at the September year-to-date [F15], so this is a seasonal production pipeline rather than dead stock. It eases to 1.00x by FY2030E because inventory was flat year-to-date while revenue rose 17.9% [F14/F16] and management says it tightened inventory policy after the FY2025 build [S3].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 22% statutory rate under UU HPP (macro deck tax_rate_id); FY2025 effective was 53.7/243.7 = 22.0%, so the statutory rate is what the LK shows being paid.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt
assumptions.basis: 9.5% = 7.45% 10-year SUN risk-free plus the house 200bp corporate spread (macro deck). Debt is almost nil (IDR 16.8bn at FY2025), so this line is immaterial to value; FY2025 finance costs were IDR 66m.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 2.5%: FY2025 interest income of IDR 16.8bn on opening cash of IDR 567.7bn = 3.0%, but 9M-2026 finance income fell to IDR 5.2bn as the cash balance halved, implying about 2%. Deposits and current-account interest only.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: the company is in net cash and funds the seasonal inventory build from its own balance sheet; the only bank line is a small working-capital facility (IDR 16.8bn drawn at FY2025).

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero as a below-EBIT line, because the audited statements have none: FY2025 profit before tax of 243.705 is operating profit 226.930 plus finance income 16.841 less finance cost 0.066 [S3 p.88]. The charge the earlier draft put here is not below EBIT — it is the other-operating line inside operating profit, -20.701bn in FY2025 and -24.387bn in FY2024, of which inventory impairment provisioning alone is 26.894bn and 29.455bn [S3 p.158, note 29]. It is now carried in opex_pct, not zeroed.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero: minorities were -IDR 0.3bn on IDR 190.0bn of net profit in FY2025 and -IDR 0.3bn in 9M-2026, immaterial at under 5% of equity.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 42%: FY2025 declared Rp26 per share = 40.99% of parent profit [F29/F30]; FY2024 was 47.06%. The board has paid a dividend every year through a negative-cash-flow cycle, so a mid-40s payout is the revealed policy; 42% keeps a little more cash inside as working capital normalises.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: 3,000,000,000 shares in issue and no corporate action announced; the company has never done a rights issue.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3.0% nominal = 2.5% long-run IDR inflation (Bank Indonesia target midpoint, macro deck) plus 0.5% real — an agri-input franchise growing with planted area and yield, not with population-plus- productivity GDP. Deliberately below the 5% explicit-year growth and inside the 40% extreme gate.

challenges.challenge: The terminal value (Rp1,563.8bn, 43.8% of the DCF) applies g=3.0% to FY2035E FCFF of Rp124.2bn, but that FCFF is struck with 5.0% revenue growth and a Delta-NWC of Rp145.1bn (nwc_pct 1.00 x revenue 2,901.1 -> 3,046.2; fund record lines). At the stated 3.0% terminal growth Delta-NWC is Rp91.4bn and terminal FCFF is Rp177.9bn (EBIT 396.0 x 0.78 + D&A 100.5 - capex 140.1 - 91.4), giving TV ~Rp2,240bn and a DCF of ~Rp647/share, not Rp561. That 15% understatement of the primary method alone takes the blend from Rp623 to ~Rp687 and the expected return to ~+19%, i.e. ADD not HOLD. This is an arithmetic inconsistency between the growth embedded in the terminal cash flow and the growth rate applied to it, not a disagreement on judgment.
challenges.answer: Correct, and it was arithmetic not judgement. Revenue growth now tapers 5.0/4.5/4.0/3.5/3.0% over FY2031E-FY2035E with lt=3.0%=terminal, so the FY2035E FCFF the Gordon formula capitalises embeds 3% growth; the terminal delta-NWC is now the 1.0x working-capital ratio on a 3% revenue increment, not the 5% one. The DCF rises from the red team figure of about Rp561 to Rp777.9 and the target from Rp536.5 to Rp697.0, moving the rating from HOLD to BUY [S0]

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA leg (Rp807, 25% weight) is priced on metric 293.388, which fund record shows is FY2025A EBITDA (year to 31 Dec 2025), yet section 4 calls it "LTM EBITDA" and they are not the same thing as at the 30 Sep 2026 balance-sheet date. LTM operating profit is FY2025A 237.65 - 9M2025 99.595 + 9M2026 79.174 = 217.2 [S2 p.6], plus ~Rp57bn LTM D&A gives ~Rp274bn; FY2026E EBITDA is Rp234.7bn. At 7.133x the leg is ~Rp763 (LTM) or ~Rp667 (FY2026E), not Rp807 - the highest of the three plausible bases. On FY2026E the blend falls to ~Rp588 and the target to ~Rp510, below the Rp515 price.
challenges.answer: Accepted on the label and the arithmetic. The leg is priced on FY2025A audited EBITDA of 293.4, not LTM; the prose now says so and states the LTM basis (FY2025A EBIT less the nine months of 2025 plus the nine months of 2026) and the FY2026E trough EBITDA. On FY2026E the leg is about Rp664 and the blend about Rp637, a total return near 27%, still above the ADD threshold. The headline target uses the engine metric, which I may not edit [S2, F45, F46]

challenges.challenge: The sensitivity exhibit published at section 4 is the PLANTATIONS default, not a BISI sensitivity: fund record sensitivities are "benchmark price (CPO x0.8-1.2) vs IDR/USD" and "volume x0.9-1.1 vs cost intensity / strip ratio", and all 50 cells print 673.243002 - identical to the undiscounted base target - because the model has no a.volume, a.strip_ratio or CPO driver (drivers_used {}). The paragraph immediately above tells the reader the table shows the gross-margin and working-capital sensitivities; it shows neither, and a flat grid tells a reader the value is insensitive to everything.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The grid is a PLANTATIONS config default whose axes are a palm-oil benchmark, a volume driver and a strip ratio, none of which exist in this model, so all fifty cells print the undiscounted base. I cannot edit config or the engine, so I deleted the exhibit and the sentence describing it and say plainly in section 4 why no grid is published [S0]

challenges.challenge: The bear case (25%, Rp541) shocks only gross_margin -1.5pp and nwc_pct +0.08, but the fund record bear narrative says "the high-cost inventory is marked down" and section 5 itself says a one-tenth markdown of the Rp872.7bn corn-seed WIP [F15] is ~Rp87bn pre-tax, about half of FY2026E net profit of Rp136.0bn. No write-down shock and no volume/revenue shock exist anywhere in the scenario set, although sections 2 and 5 say El Nino cuts the 2026/27 season twice. The published bear is a margin-only bear, not the bear the report describes.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The bear now shocks revenue growth by -3pp (the El Nino volume) and gross margin by -3pp, which carries the seed work-in-process markdown because a one-off has no line in a driver model; the bull mirrors both at +3pp. The narrative and section 5 say exactly this and no longer claim a markdown the model does not run [S2, F15]

challenges.challenge: Section 5 says "Our three cases are mirrored on the same two drivers", but nwc_pct is shocked +0.08 in the bear and -0.06 in the bull (fund record valuation.scenarios), an unsourced two-point asymmetry, and qc_justifications is {} so no reason or source is recorded. The bear is harder than the bull by construction, which is exactly the asymmetry the house card requires to be sourced.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The working-capital shock is now mirrored at plus or minus 0.08 in bear and bull, the section 5 claim is corrected, and the reason is recorded in qc_justifications so the auditor reads it rather than the prose [S3, F14]

challenges.challenge: No asset-value case is run. At 30 Sep 2026 current assets are Rp2,769.9bn against current liabilities of Rp278.8bn - about Rp2,491bn of net current assets - for a market capitalisation of Rp1,545bn (price Rp515 x 3.0bn shares), and net cash alone is Rp335.1bn or Rp111.7/share, 21.7% of the price. The bull case tops out at Rp795, below book value of Rp1,164, and the P/B leg was dropped rather than tested at a justified multiple. For a controlled, cash-rich name trading at 0.62x net current assets, the absence of any asset-backed upside case is a missing bull argument.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 4 now states that net current assets exceed the market capitalisation and that the shares trade below the working capital in the business, and explains why we do not run it as a valuation case: the inventory is seed work-in-process at cost, not a commodity stock with a resale floor. The asset backing does its work in the bull, whose narrative now carries it [S2, F13, F15, F32]

challenges.challenge: BISI's free float is 12.41%, below the 15.0% minimum in the house registry (fund record valuation.konglo.profile.free_float: compliant false, tier "mcap below Rp5tn", source S25). Sections 1, 5 and 6 cite 12.4% only as a liquidity haircut; the report never says the name fails the house's own free-float test, and never discusses remediation (a controlling-shareholder sell-down or placement) or what it would do to supply and index eligibility.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Sections 5 and 6 now state the fifteen per cent house minimum, that the free float fails it, the 2029 compliance date, the sell-down or placement remediation route and its supply effect on a stock trading this thinly. Reflected as a governance and supply risk, not only as a liquidity haircut [S2, F33]

challenges.challenge: Section 2 says "the deck inputs that do reach this model are the macro ones, the rupiah and consumer-price inflation" and section 5 says a sustained rupiah depreciation raises COGS, but fund record drivers_used is {} - no deck variable is linked to revenue, margin, capex or working capital - and the IDR/USD sensitivity grid is flat at 673.243. The desk's agricultural deck does carry corn (FY2027E 214.57 vs spot 174.11), the crop that sets both BISI's seed demand and its seed-corn input cost, and the model uses none of it. The model therefore reads no deck variables at all, contrary to the method card and to section 2.
challenges.answer: Right on the fact: drivers_used is empty because the corporate template has no commodity-price linkage, so no deck series reaches revenue, margin or capex. I corrected the section 2 claim instead of pretending a link exists, name corn FY2027E against spot as context, and keep FX and corn as risks in section 5 [S3, S0]

challenges.challenge: FY2027E revenue grows +6.0% (Rp1,908.5bn to Rp2,023.0bn) with no volume shock, although sections 2 and 5 say the 2026/27 El Nino season cuts seed volume "twice" and BPS reports September corn output -6.46% on a weaker Q4 [S6]. Separately, the gross-margin recovery to 35.5% / 36.0% is justified only by "the high-cost seed crop clears" - clearing high-cost inventory at market prices lowers, not raises, the margin; the recovery needs a lower 2026/27 seed production cost, which is unsourced. This is the largest value driver in the model and it is asserted, not evidenced.
challenges.answer: Accepted on both halves. FY2027E growth is cut to 4.0% for the shortened 2026/27 season, and the margin recovery is re-based on a segment mix path - vegetable seed at a 58.64% FY2025 margin growing with the Chia Tai joint venture - not on the high-cost crop clearing, which I agree was wrong logic [S3, F42, F7]

flags.message: expected return +67%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Expected return of 66.5% is the DCF of 935.2 a share against the 492.0 price, and three sourced drivers produce it: FY2026E gross margin of 33.5% recovering to 38.0% by FY2035E on the mix path from the 9M-2026 corn-seed trough of 24.1% [S2, F18/F19; S3, F23/F24]; working capital falling from 1.17x of revenue to 1.00x as inventory stays flat while sales grow [S2, F14/F31; S3]; and a 51.8% terminal-value share at g=3.0% [S0]. The DCF is recomputed on the fixed-cost opex base (FY2026E 23.3% of sales, not the 25.2% nine-month ratio applied to a year whose Q4 carries 34% of revenue), so no part of the return comes from a lower margin assumption. Reverse DCF, holding the other drivers at base: at our 38.0% long-run margin the Rp492 price implies a working-capital ratio near 2.0x of revenue rather than the 1.00x we model (the DCF at 2.0x is Rp505; each 10pp of working capital is worth about IDR49 a share); at our working-capital path it implies a long-run gross margin of about 31%, below even the 33.5% FY2026E trough and nine points under the FY2025A actual of 40.1% (the DCF at a 32% long-run margin is Rp537, and each point of margin is worth about IDR66 a share, roughly 7% of the DCF). The price is therefore pricing a permanent working-capital sink or a margin below the trough as the long run — not disputing the direction of the recovery.
